entries.api: profile=direct_cpp registered installed message pub/sub slice
entries.notes: On Jazzy/Cyclone, early activation replaces the default String/UInt64 imports and explicitly registered canonical package/msg/Message interfaces with actual generated C++ classes. Installed rosidl metadata, generated headers, canonical cppyy aliases, and C++ typesupport are required; nested message dependencies are resolved before aliases change. One NativeSession owns the rclcpp node, publisher, subscription, and executor for the common subclassed Node, integer-depth entity, and spin/spin_once pattern. Publishing uses the exact C++ object. Baseline callbacks receive one owning C++ copy; the subscription_shared_lease option instead shares the received allocation with zero MessageT deep copies. One- and two-argument callback shapes expose either the message alone or that same generated C++ message plus native rclcpp MessageInfo fields. All routes poison and avoid generated-Python conversion and serialization, retain callback values safely, and support native callback groups and the direct public single-threaded executor. Python message classes, stale imports, missing interfaces, unsupported QoS/options, and uncovered operations fail closed. Five clean x86-64 Jazzy/Cyclone characterization runs cover flat String and nested Header at 1 and 10 kHz with verified C++ markers and no case failures; direct combined CPU is substantially below stock, while the lease has no consistent CPU advantage over the C++ copy. A ten-repetition MessageInfo relay characterization records 0.190x stock-info relay CPU and 0.288x combined CPU with zero conversions or serialization calls. The incomplete surface remains experimental, and raw shared-host artifacts are descriptive rather than release claims.

entries.api: Node.create_timer(period, Python callback)
entries.notes: Stock timer authority is explicit. The corpus covers callback groups, autostart=false, reset, callback execution, cancellation, exception propagation, and destruction; required_cpp rejects before creation.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp Node.create_timer including inspection, autostart=False, cancel/reset/destroy, spin, and spin_once
entries.notes: On Jazzy/Cyclone, the opt-in profile creates a real rclcpp GenericTimer on the node's own ROS clock (sim-time-aware, matching stock's create_timer(clock=None) default) via the NativeSession executor, and enters the Python callback once per firing without message conversion, serialization, or a per-firing data copy. is_ready delegates to TimerBase::is_ready, time_until_next_call uses TimerBase::time_until_trigger and maps the canceled nanoseconds-max sentinel to None, and time_since_last_call reads rcl_timer_get_time_since_last_call from the exact native handle. Pre-fire, post-fire, canceled, reset, destroyed-handle, and stable timer_period_ns behavior pass with conversion and serialization poisoned. Default clock, callback groups, continuous periodic use, and native autostart=false construction followed by reset are covered. clock=None and clock=node.get_clock() are both honored -- the node's own clock is the only clock a DirectClock can ever wrap -- while a standalone or foreign clock argument fails closed before entity creation, as does any unexpected keyword argument (create_timer's signature now matches stock's exactly, with no **options catch-all). Verified live: a frozen, never-published /clock leaves a 0.5s-sim-period timer never firing while wall time passes well beyond that period; advancing /clock in explicit steps fires the callback only once sim time crosses the period; a use_sim_time=False node's timer fires on system time within a bounded wall interval; and destroying the facade stops delivery while the executor keeps spinning. The route remains experimental.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp Node.create_rate()/destroy_rate() returning a DirectRate over the node's NativeClockSleeper
entries.notes: create_rate(frequency, clock=None) validates frequency > 0 (ValueError, matching stock's message) and honors only the node's own clock or None (a foreign clock argument fails closed); it returns a DirectRate(rclpy.timer.Rate) anchored at the node clock's now() plus one period. sleep() blocks on the node's NativeClockSleeper (the same primitive clock.direct_cpp_sleep proves) with its own fixed-rate bookkeeping -- the rclcpp::Rate algorithm, including the catch-up guard that resyncs to now()+period after a stall of more than one period instead of bursting zero-length sleeps -- rather than stock's Timer+threading.Event design, so backend is mixed (native sleep, Python schedule tracking), not pure cpp. Verified live with forbidden_boundary poisoned: isinstance(rclpy.timer.Rate); five successive sleeps at 10 Hz land within tolerance of five periods with no per-gap drift, matching an in-process stock Rate/Timer/executor sibling's own cadence over the same iteration count; sim-time pacing that resolves only once a native /clock publish crosses the anchored deadline, not on wall time; a context shutdown waking an in-flight sleep with ROSInterruptException rather than blocking forever; and a destroyed rate's sleep() raising RuntimeError. This is a documented behavioral superset of stock Rate, never a deficit: DirectRate sleeps correctly with or without a spinning executor, where stock's Rate blocks forever without one (the suite's own background-executor-thread profile for the clock timer was left unproven, so this route deliberately avoids depending on it). The rclpy.timer.Rate/rclpy.node.Rate class symbols are not patched -- a directly-constructed stock Rate keeps running unmodified stock code; only create_rate()'s own facade is accelerated.

entries.api: rclpy.spin_once(accelerated_node, timeout_sec=...)
entries.notes: The wrapper delegates to stock execution and reports Python authority. Timer, subscription, service, and guard callback exceptions preserve their exact user-defined Python types.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp Executor/SingleThreadedExecutor ownership and top-level spin APIs
entries.notes: On Jazzy/Cyclone, direct nodes start unowned and can be added, removed, or transferred between public SingleThreadedExecutor facades backed by exact rclcpp executors. Top-level spin, spin_once, spin_until_future_complete, blocked-wait wake, context-manager shutdown, callback exceptions, node destruction, and generated-C++ pub/sub and Future completion are covered. Repeated global spin_once retains native membership without exposing logical membership, avoiding per-call executor guard churn. The corrected ten-repetition characterization records 0.260x stock CPU for explicit ownership and 0.322x for the source-compatible global route, but the explicit facade remains 1.279x its raw rclcpp control and therefore has no raw-parity claim. MultiThreadedExecutor construction stays fail-closed; create_task no longer fails closed (see executor.direct_cpp_tasks).

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp default, mutually-exclusive, and reentrant native callback groups
entries.notes: The direct Node exposes its real rclcpp default group and lazily binds explicit mutually-exclusive or reentrant facades to their first native node. Publishers, subscriptions including lease and MessageInfo routes, timers, services, clients, and action clients pass the exact native group through rclcpp options or overloads. Cross-node reuse fails before entity creation and group/entity lifetimes are retained through teardown. Single-threaded execution is covered; concurrent callback-group behavior remains unclaimed while MultiThreadedExecutor is fail-closed.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp Executor.create_task/Task/coroutine driving over create_future
entries.notes: create_task() is no longer fail-closed: a plain callable or a coroutine handed to the direct SingleThreadedExecutor runs to completion (or suspends on an awaited Future and resumes through the Future's own done-callback machinery), driven by _drive_tasks() ahead of each native spin step. A raising task re-raises on the calling thread from spin()/spin_once(), matching stock's own re-raise-after-run behavior, not just via future.result(). spin_until_future_complete() ends cleanly on a future a task itself resolves. A differential test runs the identical coroutines under a genuine stock SingleThreadedExecutor and the direct one and requires identical result/exception/suspend outcomes. One scenario -- cancelling a task before its first drive -- is proven direct-only, not in the differential: stock rclpy 7.1.11 itself raises a KeyError from its own _wait_for_ready_callbacks bookkeeping in that exact scenario (a pre-existing stock limitation, reproducible with zero direct_cpp involvement), which this facade's simpler task-queue design does not share. MultiThreadedExecutor construction stays fail-closed.

entries.api: MultiThreadedExecutor with reentrant and mutually exclusive callback groups
entries.notes: A two-thread MultiThreadedExecutor with a reentrant callback group, shutdown, status reporting, exception preservation, and required_cpp rejection is covered by differential evidence. The stock executor remains authoritative; custom Executor subclasses and sustained cross-architecture stress are not implied.

entries.api: Custom Executor subclasses, overridden scheduling internals, and sustained cross-architecture stress
entries.notes: Selected stock executor extensions are covered separately. Arbitrary Executor overrides can bypass or conflict with patched methods, and sustained workload evidence across architectures remains incomplete.

entries.api: profile=optimized bounded rclpy and stock executor spin waits
entries.notes: Fifteen fresh x86-64 processes receive SIGTERM immediately from an active callback across global, direct single-threaded, and direct multi-threaded spin; all exit cleanly and prove structured policy, signature, and ownership invariants. The 100 ms bound adds periodic idle wake-ups. ARM64 and sustained middleware-matrix evidence remain required before promotion.

entries.api: rclpy.task.Future set_result/set_exception/cancel completion
entries.notes: Future completion remains stock-authoritative under every policy to avoid destabilizing executor internals and per-callback overhead. Fresh-process tests prove exact stock set_result, set_exception, and cancel method identity for compatible, publisher_cpp, required_cpp, and optimized profiles; behavioral parity covers results, exceptions, cancellation, and done callbacks.

entries.api: Node.create_guard_condition/GuardCondition.trigger/destroy_guard_condition
entries.notes: Stock guard-condition identity, callback groups, trigger/dispatch, destruction, compatible status, bounded warnings, signature preservation, and required_cpp rejection before creation are covered.

entries.api: Node.create_service/create_client and service spinning
entries.notes: A local SetBool client/server request, Future response, callback group, discovery, status, identity, and teardown match stock. required_cpp rejects user service/client creation before side effects while preserving constructor-owned services.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp registered installed service create_service/create_client, call_async, and spin_until_future_complete
entries.notes: On Jazzy/Cyclone, early activation replaces the default SetBool and explicitly registered canonical package/srv/Service Request and Response aliases with actual generated C++ classes and creates real rclcpp service/client entities. Installed services and nested message dependencies are resolved before transactional alias mutation; missing, stale, and unregistered types fail before graph creation. The common synchronous two-argument callback, call_async/Future, and stock-shaped blocking call with a servicing executor on another thread work with default service QoS: callback requests are owning C++ copies, responses are assigned in C++, client requests make one native C++ value copy, and returned results remain C++. There is no Python-message conversion or serialization bridge. Each operation uses an unmodified stock rclpy.task.Future only as Python control state; no global Future method is patched. Blocking call timeout removes the native pending request, and callback use retains the stock deadlock warning. Custom QoS/groups, coroutine callbacks, introspection, and manual response send fail closed. SetBool plus explicitly registered Trigger are covered by stock and compiled rclcpp peers in both directions, cancellation, timeouts, exceptions, retained values, status authority, teardown, and reinitialization. A clean five-repetition x86-64 Trigger client characterization records median paired direct/stock ratios of 0.218x CPU, 0.373x p50, 0.429x p99, and 2.634x throughput with exact C++ and no-conversion markers. The bounded surface remains experimental pending broader service API coverage, dedicated-host thresholds, and ARM64 measurement.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp LookupTransform ActionClient async goal, feedback, result, and cancel slice
entries.notes: On Jazzy/Cyclone, early direct_cpp activation keeps the default tf2_msgs/action/LookupTransform client and accepts explicitly registered canonical installed actions. Goal, Feedback, Result, UUID, SendGoal/GetResult request and response, feedback-message, CancelGoal request and response, and nested payload aliases are validated transactionally and replaced with their actual generated C++ classes. A custom nested Accumulate action passes fresh-cache interoperability against a compiled rclcpp_action server, retains C++ values after teardown, and links its installed typesupport with an explicit RUNPATH. A real rclcpp_action client and batched C++ readiness snapshot drive send_goal_async, feedback callbacks, get_result_async, and cancel_goal_async without generated-Python message conversion or serialization. Goal acceptance/rejection, exactly ordered feedback, success, cancellation, retained values, graph identity, callback exceptions, endpoint loss, teardown, and reinitialization are covered. Missing, stale, and unregistered actions fail before graph creation; custom goal UUIDs, non-default action QoS, synchronous calls, introspection, and uncovered options remain fail-closed. Historical characterization used unequal feedback QoS and remains invalid as current evidence. The corrected clean five-repetition artifact build/action-client-cyclone-b2f0f2d-corrected.json uses identical public QoS and source/executor shape and records median paired direct/stock ratios of 0.2606 CPU, 0.7138/0.3283 accept p50/p99, 0.9848/0.9647 result p50/p99, and 1.0160 throughput. All direct samples retain exact C++ authority, arm 16 boundary tripwires, record zero conversion/serialization/CDR calls, and tear down cleanly. Claims remain disabled pending dedicated-host and ARM64 repetition. This remains a bounded experimental client slice pending broader action-client API coverage and a custom-action performance workload.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp ActionServer synchronous goal/cancel/accepted/execute callbacks, feedback, result, and cancellation slice
entries.notes: On Jazzy/Cyclone, the direct ActionServer keeps Goal, Feedback, Result, UUID, action envelopes, accepted-goal state, and rclcpp_action server authority in C++. Synchronous Python callbacks receive the exact generated C++ values; converters and serializers are poisoned in the live proof. Server-first executor polling covers acceptance, staged feedback, success, rejection, cancellation, default abort, callback errors, deferred accepted goals, retained values, safe deferred server close, teardown, and reinitialization. An unchanged external stock rclpy ActionClient also drives payload-rich goal, feedback, and result traffic through the direct server while every server-side application value remains exact generated C++ and retained after teardown. Node or context teardown attempted inside an active server callback fails before mutation. The corrected clean five-repetition artifact build/action-server-cyclone-b2f0f2d-corrected.json uses one common AOT client plus identical public QoS and records median paired direct/stock ratios of 0.6475 server CPU, 0.7386/0.7364 accept p50/p99, 0.9893/0.9758 result p50/p99, and 1.0107 throughput. All direct samples retain exact C++ authority, arm 16 boundary tripwires, record zero conversion/serialization/CDR calls, and tear down cleanly. The default source-compatible route performs 2,080 counted exact-C++ adapter deep copies per 520-goal sample and remains 2.588x AOT CPU, making copy/callback overhead an explicit optimization target rather than a representation conversion. Product 47e4e56 with suite 48927c9 adds explicit opt-in create_feedback_shared/create_result_shared factories plus publish_feedback_shared and succeed_shared/abort_shared/canceled_shared terminal operations. Factory-created values retain their actual generated C++ type and shared ownership; non-factory values reject, and the caller must not mutate a value concurrently with its handoff. In the bounded three-repetition, 5-warmup/30-measured-goal diagnostic, every copy sample records exactly 140 adapter deep copies while every shared sample records zero adapter deep copies, 105 feedback shared handoffs, and 35 result shared handoffs. The ratio of lane medians is a 5.09% server-CPU reduction, but one of three paired repetitions regresses and the short shared-host run is noisy. This is mechanism evidence only, not a performance claim or a change to the default path. Claims remain disabled pending the fixed full matrix, dedicated-host repetition, and ARM64 repetition. This P0 slice requires the single-threaded executor, a mutually-exclusive callback group, default action QoS, and synchronous callbacks; concurrency, coroutine callbacks, custom QoS, introspection, and uncovered options fail closed.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp owning Parameter facade plus local declare/get/type/set/atomic/describe/list and pre/on/post callbacks
entries.notes: On Jazzy/Cyclone, each rclpy-shaped Parameter facade owns one rclcpp::Parameter and local DirectNode parameter operations retain native rclcpp node authority. Parameter, ParameterValue, ParameterDescriptor, range, ListParametersResult, and SetParametersResult imports are actual generated C++ aliases; non-C++ control messages, descriptors, and callback results fail before mutation. Python values are materialized only by the explicit .value property. Each owning snapshot captures only its immutable parameter-type enum at construction; type access has no C++ crossing and .value dispatches directly to one typed C++ accessor without caching a Python scalar or message payload. A bounded plain-dict mirror holds only owning rclcpp::Parameter-backed facades; its default hit performs no cppyy call, lock, or instrumentation update. Successful local and remote post-set callbacks replace immutable snapshots before user post callbacks, rejection leaves entries unchanged, deletion invalidates, and coherence failure disables and clears only the optimization. Capacity, disabled state, opt-in hit metrics, all ten types and empty arrays, local and remote mutation, dynamic type replacement, callback ordering, retained snapshots, concurrent executor-thread writes, overrides, teardown, and reinitialization are covered with converter, serializer, and CDR tripwires at zero. Dynamic non-read-only undeclaration uses the public rclcpp operation and invalidates only the mirror entry while retained C++ snapshots remain valid. Static undeclaration and descriptor mutation fail closed because Jazzy rclcpp cannot provide the rclpy contract without semantic emulation. The CPU-first stock/direct/native-Python benchmark harness covers declare, native-object get, explicit value snapshot, and atomic set. The clean pre-optimization artifact at product a8c2cb6 with suite 852e48b records direct/stock process-CPU ratios of 0.580 for declare, 38.682 for get-native, 30.950 for get-value-snapshot, and 0.446 for atomic set. The clean Phase-1 artifact at product 6da8193 with suite 0518f37 records 0.474 for declare, 10.316 for get-native, 8.712 for get-value-snapshot, and 0.349 for atomic set; direct get CPU fell 73.5% to 1,223 ns/op but still failed the stock CPU priority. The clean Phase-2 artifact at product 72e28b5 with suite 0518f37 records 0.6857 for declare, 0.5633 for get-native, 1.3433 for get-value-snapshot, and 0.5205 for atomic set; snapshot median CPU is 207 ns/op versus 157 ns/op stock. The clean Phase-3 artifact at product 0faa435 with suite 941d6ce records 0.6943 for declare, 0.6090 for get-native, 1.1073 for get-value-snapshot, and 0.5148 for atomic set; snapshot median CPU is 167 ns/op versus 152 ns/op stock. Performance claims remain disabled because explicit snapshot CPU still misses the stock priority.

Importing AsyncParameterClient before direct activation rejects activation. Clean five-repetition artifact build/remote-parameter-cyclone-be024c2.json records direct/stock combined process-CPU ratios of 0.1583 for get-one and 0.2492 for set-atomically-one, with 6.3175x and 4.0148x throughput respectively. All direct samples retain exact generated C++ values with boundary counters at zero; claims remain disabled pending dedicated-host and ARM64 repetition. entries.api: profile=direct_cpp rclpy.wait_for_message with default or explicit QoS and timeout
entries.notes: On Jazzy/Cyclone, early direct_cpp activation installs a functools.wraps facade over the installed rclpy.wait_for_message function, retaining its public module, name, documentation, signature, and unwrap target. The synchronous call creates a temporary direct rclcpp subscription and native single-threaded executor when needed; successful default- and explicit-QoS calls return the actual generated C++ message, and finite and zero timeouts retain the stock (False, None) shape. Fresh-process stock/direct differential coverage proves temporary-subscription cleanup, retained-message lifetime after node/session teardown, released executor ownership, and zero conversion, serialization, and CDR poison calls. Jazzy's installed implementation itself cannot execute over a direct node because it hard-codes _rclpy.WaitSet and stock subscription handles. A same-thread recursive call from the node's active single-threaded executor callback therefore fails before creating a temporary subscription; raw WaitSet/guard-condition APIs, multi-threaded execution, and broader waitable behavior are not claimed. The unchanged stock-authoritative entry remains the default compatible-profile authority, and no CPU result or performance claim is attached to this bounded direct slice.

entries.api: Time.to_msg/from_msg and Duration.to_msg/from_msg under profile=direct_cpp
entries.notes: Time and Duration are unchanged stock rclpy classes under direct_cpp; to_msg/from_msg are not patched. rclpy's time.py/duration.py resolve their builtin_interfaces.msg.Time/Duration return annotations at import time (no future-annotations deferral), and direct_cpp has already installed generated C++ builtin_interfaces.msg.Time_<...>/Duration_<...> aliases by then, so the same unchanged stock bodies construct and read the C++ message: keyword construction, .sec/.nanosec access, and the from_msg isinstance check all work against the C++ type with no product shim. Verified with forbidden_boundary poisoned: to_msg()/from_msg() round-trip correctly for both Time and Duration, and a to_msg() payload assigned into a generated C++ Header.stamp field keeps the C++ type end to end, proving a real app timestamp path never crosses to a Python message or a serialization boundary. This is an intentional divergence from stock's Python builtin_interfaces payload, not a defect; the corresponding 12 from_msg/to_msg ledger rows stay missing_mismatch by design (the payload type genuinely differs) and are not annotated.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp Node.get_clock() returning a native-node-backed Clock/ROSClock
entries.notes: DirectNode.get_clock() retains one DirectClock/DirectROSClock per node, backed by the native foundation's NativeNodeClock -- the node's exact rclcpp::Clock (node clocks are always RCL_ROS_TIME). DirectClock/DirectROSClock subclass stock rclpy.clock.Clock/ROSClock for isinstance identity but bypass Clock.__new__ so no second, disconnected _rclpy.Clock is created. now() returns a stock rclpy.time.Time built from the native now_nanoseconds() hot path; clock_type is resolved once at construction and cached, so it never re-touches the native object. Verified live with forbidden_boundary poisoned: isinstance/identity (one clock per node, the same object returned on every get_clock() call), a stock-time differential against time.time_ns(), address identity against the node's own native rclcpp::Clock, and clean teardown (destroy_node() closes the retained clock; a later now() raises instead of touching a dangling native reference). A fast in-process unit test additionally proves the wrapper checks closedness before calling into the native object at all. Standalone Clock(...) construction, the raw handle, jump callbacks, and set_ros_time_override are explicit_fail_closed -- the native foundation does not support them yet -- rather than silently falling back to a disconnected stock clock. sleep_for/sleep_until are the one accelerated exception on a node-bound clock; see clock.direct_cpp_sleep.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp use_sim_time + /clock activation through Node.get_clock()
entries.notes: use_sim_time is an already-landed parameter: setting it via parameter_overrides at construction or set_parameters afterward reaches the real rclcpp parameter machinery with no direct_cpp-specific wiring, so the node's own native rclcpp::TimeSource (attached to every rclcpp::Node, not a product reimplementation) owns activation, /clock delivery, and deactivation exactly as it does for stock. Verified live: parameter_overrides activates ros_time_is_active synchronously at construction (matching stock); publishing rosgraph_msgs/msg/Clock on /clock (registered via interfaces=) drives now() to the published value; setting use_sim_time back to false deactivates and resumes wall time. A stock rclpy sibling process run immediately afterward (sim-time's /clock topic name is fixed and process-wide, so the two scenarios never run concurrently) produces identical activation/deactivation observations and reaches the same simulated nanoseconds value. rclpy.time_source.TimeSource is not patched and not needed; attaching it to a direct_cpp node is a harmless no-op (no clock is ever associated with it), but explicitly attaching a direct clock to it hits the same fail-closed set_ros_time_override every other manual-override path raises -- proven directly rather than half-wiring a second, competing time source.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp Node.get_clock().sleep_for/sleep_until over the node's NativeClockSleeper
entries.notes: A node-bound DirectClock's sleep_for/sleep_until run rclcpp::Clock::sleep_for/sleep_until natively over a per-node NativeClockSleeper (lazily created and cached, closed before the clock at node teardown): ROS-time-aware (paced by /clock under use_sim_time, not wall/steady time), and interruptible by context shutdown (returns False and wakes early, matching stock's own sleep contract) rather than by any product-level cancellation. Verified live with forbidden_boundary poisoned: a wall-time sleep matching an in-process stock Clock/Context sleep of the same duration; a sim-time sleep_until that resolves only once a native /clock publish crosses the target, not on stale wall/steady time; a long sleep_for that a context shutdown wakes early and false; a fresh sleep_for on the now-shut-down context raising stock's own NotInitializedException up front; and native clock-identity (the sleeper retains the exact same rclcpp::Clock the node's own clock wraps). A clock built without a sleeper_provider (never produced by Node.get_clock(), only reachable via the internal _wrap used in fast unit tests) fails sleep closed with a typed error instead of silently no-op'ing, and a foreign, non-active context argument is rejected the same way (direct_cpp has exactly one context per process). Jump callbacks, the raw handle, set_ros_time_override, and standalone Clock(...) construction remain explicit_fail_closed and are unchanged by this entry (see time.direct_cpp_node_clock); the native sleeper already handles time-source jumps internally (rclcpp::Clock::sleep_for/sleep_until wake on a jump via their own C++ ClockEvent), so this is a narrow, deliberate exception to the fail-closed clock surface, not a claim that jump callbacks work.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp rclpy.type_support validators (check_for_type_support, check_is_valid_srv_type, check_is_valid_msg_type) over stock types whose type tree reaches a direct-rebound cppyy message, and over registered direct message aliases themselves
entries.notes: On Jazzy/Cyclone, direct_messages.install mirrors a lazy, read-only _TYPE_SUPPORT identity capsule onto the metaclass of every direct-rebound cppyy message, sourced from the stock metaclass it replaced. This makes check_for_type_support and check_is_valid_srv_type succeed for any stock type whose generated type-support import transitively walks a rebound field: std_srvs.srv.SetBool, all four lifecycle services (ChangeState/GetState/GetAvailableStates/GetAvailableTransitions), and the auto-generated <Service>_Event message's ServiceEventInfo.stamp field all reach the rebound builtin_interfaces.msg.Time (pulled in by the default tf2_msgs/action/LookupTransform -> action_msgs/msg/GoalInfo.stamp dependency closure). Verified live with the C++ message-conversion boundary poisoned: SetBool, the four lifecycle services, ServiceEventInfo (transitive walk target), and Time itself (direct manifestation) all validate cleanly, the alias is unchanged (Time remains the exact cppyy class), and two distinct rebound messages carry distinct metaclasses with independent _TYPE_SUPPORT state. Only the identity capsule is exposed; asserted absent are the four conversion capsules (_CREATE_ROS_MESSAGE/_CONVERT_FROM_PY/_CONVERT_TO_PY/_DESTROY_ROS_MESSAGE), since a cppyy object exposes its fields as plain Python attributes and those capsules would otherwise round-trip a rebound message through stock C conversion -- a silent conversion bridge on a path that claims to be accelerated. check_is_valid_msg_type is additionally patched (signature preserved) to accept a registered direct message alias -- identity-matched against the active installation's bindings, after running check_for_type_support for its import side effect -- and to delegate everything else, including a genuinely non-message type (a stock service class), to stock, which rejects it with its precise RuntimeError; the patched validator carries no direct-backend ledger authority since rclpy.type_support functions are not introspected as direct, so its ledger row stays unassessed. serialize_message/deserialize_message over a rebound message remain a separate, pre-existing gap this slice does not bridge. restore() removes exactly the attributes it added.

entries.api: profile=direct_cpp LifecycleNode construction
entries.notes: This is a reviewed, deliberately fail-closed block, not an omission: LifecycleNode(LifecycleNodeMixin, Node) subclasses whatever Node currently is, and direct_cpp rebinds rclpy.node.Node to DirectNode, which owns a native rclcpp node and has no handle attribute at all. LifecycleNodeMixin.__init__ needs self.handle to construct _rclpy.LifecycleStateMachine -- a stock pybind node handle the direct backend does not and cannot own -- so even after type-support validation over the four lifecycle service types is fixed (type_support.direct_rebound_validation), construction hits a second, deeper wall: a raw AttributeError at self.handle. LifecycleNode.__init__ is patched under direct_cpp to raise a precise BackendUnavailableError('lifecycle nodes are not yet supported under the direct_cpp profile') before any node work, converting that cryptic AttributeError into an honest, fail-closed block. Verified live: construction raises exactly that error -- never AttributeError, never the type-support crash -- and no partial node, publisher, or runtime registration occurs; the guard fires regardless of whether rclpy.lifecycle was imported before or after activation and is removed cleanly on deactivate. This is the manifest's first entry recorded as unsupported: full lifecycle parity needs a native lifecycle state machine over the rclcpp node and a real node-handle surface -- a large, separate lane -- and is explicitly planned future work, not a gap that went unreviewed.
